prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My mother the queen is dead. My father the king is old. He fumbles his cirque of gold And dreams of a year long fled. The young men stare at my face, But cannot meet my glance— Cavan tall as a lance, Orra swift in the race. Death was ever my price, Since my maidenhood began: At the thought of a Gaelic man My heart is sister of ice. ’Tis another for whom I wait, Though I have not kissed his sword: He or none is my lord, Though our night be soon or late. The star grows great in my breast: It is crying clearly now To the star on the burnished prow Of his galley far in the West. The capes of the North are dim, And the windward beaches smoke Where the last long roller spoke The tidings it held of him. Sorrow I know he brings, Battle, despair and change,— Beauty cruel and strange, And the shed bright blood of kings. Breast, be white for his sake! Mouth, be red for the kiss! Soul, be strong for your bliss! Heart, be ready to break!

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: And, The, But

outputs.L1:
My mother, the queen, is dead.  
My father, the king, is old.  
He fumbles his cirque of gold  
And dreams of a year long fled.

The young men stare at my face,  
Yet cannot meet my glance—  
Cavan, tall as a lance;  
Orra, swift in the race.

Death has ever been my price  
Since my maidenhood began:  
At the thought of a Gaelic man,  
My heart is a sister to ice.

’Tis another for whom I wait,  
Though I have not kissed his sword:  
He, or none, shall be my lord,  
Whether our night comes soon or late.

The star grows great in my breast;  
It is crying clearly now  
To the star on the burnished prow  
Of his galley, far in the West.

The capes of the North are dim,  
And the windward beaches smoke,  
Where the last long roller spoke  
The tidings it bore of him.

Sorrow, I know, he brings—  
Battle, despair, and change;  
Beauty, cruel and strange;  
And the bright, shed blood of kings.

Breast, be white for his sake!  
Mouth, be red for the kiss!  
Soul, be strong for your bliss!  
Heart, be ready to break!
outputs.L2:
The queen, my mother, has passed away,  
and my father, the aging king,  
turns his golden circlet uncertainly  
while recalling a year long gone.

Young suitors gaze upon me,  
yet none can hold my eyes—  
not Cavan, straight and tall as a spear,  
nor Orra, fleetest in the contest.

From the first days of womanhood,  
death has always been the cost of winning me.  
When I consider any Gaelic man,  
my heart turns cold as a sister to frost.

I am waiting for someone else,  
though my lips have never touched his blade.  
Only he shall be my master,  
whether our meeting comes early or late.

A star swells within my breast,  
calling out with sudden clarity  
to the star fixed upon the gleaming bow  
of his ship, far away in the western sea.

The northern headlands fade in haze,  
and spray clouds the shores facing the wind,  
where the final immense wave broke  
and delivered its news of him.

I know he will come bearing grief:  
warfare, hopelessness, and upheaval;  
a fierce and unfamiliar beauty,  
and the brilliant spilled blood of monarchs.

Let my breast remain pale for him.  
Let my mouth be crimson for his kiss.  
Let my spirit endure the joy awaiting it.  
Let my heart prepare to shatter.
outputs.L3:
The speaker grieves for her dead mother while watching her father, the aging king, retreat ever more deeply into memories of the past. Though she is surrounded by young Gaelic noblemen who admire her and hope to win her hand, she feels no affection for any of them. The prospect of marrying one of these suitors leaves her cold, for she believes that her fate lies elsewhere.

Instead, she waits faithfully for a distant lord whom she has never met but somehow knows is destined for her. Across the western sea, she senses his approach through an intense, almost supernatural bond, as if their lives are already joined before they have even seen one another. Yet her expectation is not entirely joyful. She understands that his coming will bring conflict and upheaval: sorrow, battle, political change, and the shedding of royal blood. Nevertheless, she accepts what awaits her, preparing herself to receive both the love he promises and the heartbreak that will accompany it.
outputs.L4:
The princess had refused every prince who came to her father’s court. They arrived beneath bright banners, bearing ivory, amber, horses, and hammered gold. One praised her beauty; another promised her dominion over valleys she had never seen. She listened with ceremonial patience, then dismissed them all. The city called her proud, but pride had little to do with it. She was waiting.

Years before, an old prophetess had taken the princess’s hands and spoken of a warrior from the West. He would cross the sea in a dark galley, she said, following a road drawn not on any chart but in the hidden designs of the gods. His sail would appear first as a black mark where the sun touched the water. Before the watchmen raised their cry, the princess would feel his coming in her blood.

The prophecy promised no gentle happiness. The warrior would carry iron, smoke, and the grief of ruined cities. His arrival would break the ordered pattern of her life. For his sake, doors would be opened that should have remained barred; vows would be abandoned; kin would turn against kin. The girl she had been would vanish, and in her place would stand a woman capable of tenderness, treachery, courage, and despair.

Still she waited.

At night she climbed the eastern tower, though the western sea lay beyond the palace roofs, and watched the stars revolve above the sleeping city. In their cold arrangements she imagined oars dipping into moonlit water. When wind worried the shutters, she heard a sail snapping taut. When storms rolled inland, she thought of bronze shields ringing beneath foreign blows.

She did not deceive herself about what love would demand. She knew the stranger might awaken her heart only to leave it desolate. He might accept her help and afterward remember duty, glory, or another home more strongly than he remembered her. The same galley that brought him could one day bear him away, shrinking against the horizon while she stood powerless on the shore.

Yet even that imagined sorrow seemed preferable to a life untouched by fate. She had no wish to be preserved like a jewel in a locked chamber. Let love wound her, if the wound revealed who she was. Let it set fire to the palace, overturn the altars, and scatter the safe years she had been offered. Better a heart broken open than one that had never answered its summons.

Then, one morning, the sea changed.

No herald had spoken. No beacon burned. But the princess woke before dawn with the taste of salt on her lips and a weight beneath her ribs, half terror and half recognition. She went alone to the highest terrace.

Far out on the reddening water, a dark sail moved toward the harbor.

The galley rose and vanished among the waves, each stroke of its oars drawing prophecy nearer. Around her, the city continued its ordinary life: servants swept courtyards, merchants lifted shutters, and doves circled the temple roofs. No one yet understood that the old order was ending.

The princess gripped the stone parapet. She saw, as if in a single vision, the warrior stepping ashore, blood on his armor and weariness in his face. She saw herself go to meet him. Behind that moment waited passion and betrayal, flight and fire, the destruction of one self and the birth of another. At the vision’s furthest edge stood a lonely shore and an empty sea.

She did not turn away.

Whatever his coming cost, it was already part of her. Love had reached her before the lover did—not as comfort, but as fate. And when the harbor bells finally began to ring, she descended from the tower to welcome both the man and the ruin that would follow him.
outputs.L5:
**And, The, But**

“The” points to something specific. “And” brings ideas together. “But” introduces contrast or change.

The road was long **and** quiet, **but** the travelers continued. They followed **the** path through the forest **and** across the hills, **but** they never lost hope. These three small words may seem ordinary, yet they shape meaning: **the** gives focus, **and** creates connection, **but** adds surprise.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic first-person poem spoken by an Irish princess who rejects local suitors while awaiting a foreign warrior destined to bring love, war, and tragedy.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Princess at the Western Window**

Let them come crowned in antler, gold, and pride—  
the princes of Connacht, the lords of Clare,  
with hounds at heel and torques upon their throats,  
their boasts blown loud as horns across the sea.

I will not have them.

I have watched their hands grow soft around the cup,  
heard every oath rehearsed beside the fire.  
They offer cattle, silver, fertile ground—  
as though my heart were acreage to bind.

My father rages.  
My mother threads her silence through the loom.  
The druids turn their faces toward the west  
and will not tell me what the ravens know.

But I have dreamed him.

Not of this green island, nor its rain,  
but salt-burned, sword-marked, foreign to our songs—  
a storm-eyed warrior on a black-prowed ship,  
with blood upon his mail and dawn behind him.

He comes for neither blessing nor for bride.  
He comes beneath another man’s command,  
bearing peace like tinder in his hands.  
Yet when he speaks, the shields will wake to thunder;  
when he touches me, the kings will go to war.

Still—I await him.

Let the sea rise white against the cliffs.  
Let every bell cry treason from the tower.  
I would rather love one hour beneath his gaze  
than live a hundred years in careful splendor.

I know the price. The dream concealed no grave.  
I saw red fields beneath a winter moon,  
a shattered harp, a crown drowned in the mud,  
his breath departing softly with my name.

And I beside him—  
not queen, not daughter, not forgiven—  
only a woman holding fast the hand  
that drew both heaven and ruin to her shore.

So send the suitors home.

Bar the gates.  
Heap the fires high above the harbor wall.  
Tonight the western wind smells sharp with iron,  
and far beyond the dark, a sail is turning.

He comes with love.  
He comes with war.

He comes for me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical ballad in rhymed quatrains about a king’s daughter who senses her beloved approaching by galley from the West.
counterfactuals.output:
The king’s fair daughter climbed the tower  
Before the dawn was red;  
“The western wind is warm tonight—  
My love comes home,” she said.  

No sail was seen beyond the foam,  
No oar flashed on the sea;  
Yet through the dark she heard a song  
That none could hear but she.  

“The gulls are wheeling toward the land,  
The tide runs silver-bright;  
His galley bears a crimson mast  
Across the folds of night.”  

The watchman gazed into the West:  
“No ship is drawing near.”  
She smiled beneath her golden veil:  
“My heart has keener ear.”  

Then out beyond the sunset’s gate,  
Where sea and heaven meet,  
A lantern glimmered like a star,  
And drums began to beat.  

The long oars struck the moonlit wave,  
The prow was crowned with flame;  
And over all the darkening deep  
The west wind spoke her name.  

She flew beneath the castle arch  
And down the salt-white strand;  
The king’s guard called, the night bells rang—  
She waited on the sand.  

At dawn the galley touched the shore,  
Her love sprang from the foam;  
And all the larks above them sang,  
“The western wind brings home.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a Celtic-inspired monologue beginning “My mother the queen is dead” and ending with the speaker commanding her heart to be ready to break.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother the queen is dead.

Before dawn, the women washed her with water drawn from the western well. They combed her silver hair with a bone comb and dressed her in the crimson cloak she wore when the hill-kings bent their knees. Now she lies beneath the rowan boughs, a gold torc at her throat and a sprig of heather between her hands.

Beyond the walls, the keeners have begun. Their voices rise and fall like winter geese above the sea. Every cry names a grief: wife, mother, judge, shield of the weak. But none names what I have lost.

She was the hand that steadied mine when first I lifted a sword. She taught me the old speech of stones, the paths of stars, and the price of every oath. She said a crown is not a circlet of gold, but a ring of iron hammered inward. I laughed then. I do not laugh now.

At sunset they will bear her through the gate. The druids will kindle the nine sacred woods, and flame will take her fair face from us. The clans will watch me for trembling. The ravens will watch me for weakness. My uncle will count my tears and reckon how soon he may seize the throne.

Let him count.

I will wear her torc. I will stand upon the king-stone barefoot, though frost splits my skin. I will swear by land and sea, by sun and moon, that no invader shall harvest our fields, no traitor shall sell our children, and no proud lord shall break the law she kept.

But first I must walk to the pyre.

First I must kiss the brow that will never again bend to mine.

The horns are sounding. The gates are opening. They are calling me queen.

Heart, be ready to break.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an archaic, mythic poem about a cold-hearted maiden whose fated lover will bring sorrow, beauty, bloodshed, and change.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Lay of the Winter-Born**

Ere yet the sun had learned his golden road,  
When elder stars kept watch o’er hill and sea,  
A maiden dwelt where winds of winter abode,  
And frost had sealed her heart eternally.  

No kindly flame within her bosom stirred,  
No lover’s song could turn her silver gaze;  
Her speech was cold, her footfall scarcely heard,  
Like moonlight wandering through a ruined place.  

Then spake the Norns beneath the ashen bough:  
*“One cometh crowned with roses, sword, and rain;  
Before his feet the proudest kings shall bow,  
And in his wake bloom loveliness and pain.*  

*He shall unbind the winter from thy breast;  
For thee shall crimson rivers stain the plain.  
Thy kiss shall grant the weary earth no rest,  
Thy tears shall fall, and nothing stay the same.”*  

So came he forth beneath a blood-red morn,  
With raven hair and eyes of storm-tossed blue;  
A wreath of dying flowers his brow did adorn,  
And from his blade the dawn’s first scarlet flew.  

He sang—and all the sleeping mountains stirred.  
He smiled—and lilies blossomed from the grave.  
He loved—and war awakened at the word,  
While banners burned above the faithless wave.  

The maiden felt her heart’s old fetters break;  
Warm grief arose where never grief had been.  
For his dear sake did realms and ages quake,  
And beauty walked where slaughter late was seen.  

Yet Fate, who weaveth joy with sable thread,  
Set love and doom together in one breath:  
He changed the world, and by her hand lay dead—  
She gained a heart, and he inherited death.  

Now spring returns where once the snows held sway,  
And red flowers climb the towers, year by year;  
But still she walks alone at close of day,  
Made mortal by one kiss, one blade, one tear.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a poem spoken by a princess with an aging royal father, unwanted Gaelic suitors, and a prophetic star in her breast calling to a distant warrior’s ship.
counterfactuals.output:
My father’s crown grows heavy with the frost;  
His hand now trembles where it once held law.  
He counts the sons of Erin, clan by clan,  
And bids me choose from hawk-eyed lords of war.

They come with torcs, with hounds, with harps of gold,  
Their Gaelic vows as proud as winter seas;  
Yet none can stir the star beneath my breast  
That burns beyond their banners and their pleas.

For nightly through my chamber’s western glass  
It wakes, and draws my spirit past the foam—  
A silver prophecy no priest can read,  
A flame that knows a sail, a sword, a name.

O distant warrior, standing at the prow,  
Though black waves rise and blind the moon above,  
My hidden star is calling to your ship—  
Come claim no kingdom; only come for love.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
